name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,769

clue.text: Time messing around with adults did this?

definitions.text: Time messing around with adults did this?

indicators.note: things messing around are out of order, so these letters get jumbled

explanation.surface: A knowing wink about grown-ups who have been fooling around together.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word does double duty: the letters are shuffled, and read straight the clue describes a romp that left everyone aroused, which is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An &lit: a spell of fooling around with other adults is exactly what gets people excited, so the whole sentence reads straight as a description.

clue.text: Guitarist's finale duckwalk after break is rubbish!

indicators.note: a finale is the closing part of a show, so take the closing letter
the guitarist's strut comes after the solo break, so its letters follow the T

blocks.note: the rolling gait of a duck

explanation.surface: A rock fan scorns the guitarist who ends a solo with a Chuck Berry duckwalk.
explanation.walkthrough: The duckwalk is Chuck Berry's famous stage strut, but here it is read literally as the way a duck gets about.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean worthless talk or nonsense.

clue.text: One in on grass crop heads of mafia outfit will eagerly rob

indicators.note: the head of each word is its front, so take the first letters

blocks.clueFragment: heads of mafia outfit will eagerly rob
blocks.note: first letters of Mafia Outfit Will Eagerly Rob

explanation.surface: A mafia gang lines up a raid on a harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads oddly because it is compressed: 'one in on grass crop' means a person or machine taking part in cutting grass short.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: crop here is the verb 'cut short', and the thing that cuts a lawn short is this machine or its operator.

clue.text: Weapon that might give fawning fellow backache?

definitions.text: that might give fawning fellow backache?

blocks.note: a medieval archer's arm, the one used at Agincourt

blocks.clueFragment: that might give fawning fellow backache?
blocks.note: a flatterer who stoops from the waist for ages ends up with a sore back; read the answer as two words

explanation.surface: A joke about a toady who bows so much his back aches.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as LONG BOW and it stops being a weapon and becomes a very drawn-out bow from the waist.
explanation.definitionFit: The first sense is a tall yew bow used in war; the second is a pun, a long bow being a lengthy obeisance.

clue.text: Game to enter town church, finding peace for a while?

indicators.note: to enter is to go into, so the game's letters go inside the others

blocks.note: T is a dictionary abbreviation for town

explanation.surface: A town rugby match is played at the church to settle a feud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Town church' reads as one building, but it is two separate abbreviations with the game slipped between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a truce is a temporary halt to fighting.

clue.text: Ecstasy-laced shot editor fancied

indicators.note: a drink laced with a drug has it mixed inside, so E goes into the shot

blocks.note: a dram is a small shot of whisky
E = the drug ecstasy, placed inside

explanation.surface: Someone thinks the editor spiked a drink with ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'shot' as a drink, not a gunshot or a photo; 'fancied' is the verb 'imagined', not 'found attractive'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to fancy something can mean to imagine it.

clue.text: Nipper close to mother in Hackney, perhaps

indicators.note: the close of a word is where it ends, so take its last letter
that letter sits in the cab

blocks.note: a hackney carriage is the official name for a London taxi

explanation.surface: A little child stays near its mum in the east London borough of Hackney.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nipper' looks like a child and Hackney like the London borough, but the answer nips with its claws and a hackney is a taxi.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: nipper is British slang for a small child, but literally anything that nips, like this pincered sea creature.

clue.text: Criminal lot rat out one who's known to sing

indicators.note: letters that are out are out of place, so rearrange them

explanation.surface: A convict informs on the whole gang, grassing like a canary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sing' is also slang for informing, which ties the definition to the criminal surface, but here it means real singing.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this voice type is the lowest female singing voice, so its owner is one known to sing.

clue.text: Country song about Hoskins heading to Nashville

indicators.note: about means around, so the song wraps around the other letters
the heading of a word is its top, so take its first letter

blocks.note: an aria is an operatic song
the setter is Hoskins, so he refers to himself

explanation.surface: A country-music song about the setter going off to Nashville.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country song' begs to be read together as country music; split it and 'Country' is the definition while 'song' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain definition by category: this is a nation in the Caucasus.

clue.text: Catch rays around excellent Welsh island

indicators.note: the tan goes around, encircling the other letters

blocks.note: you tan when you catch the sun's rays
A1 = excellent, with the 1 read as I

explanation.surface: Sunbathing on a fine Welsh island such as Anglesey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welsh island' reads as one phrase, but Welsh gives only one letter and the island is on the other side of the world.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this is an island off the coast of China.

clue.text: Junkie knocked over drug dealer for PC Handle

indicators.note: something knocked over ends up lying the other way round, so reverse it

explanation.surface: An addict mugs a dealer, and a police constable is on the case.
explanation.walkthrough: PC here is a personal computer, not a police constable, and a handle is slang for the name you go by.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: handle is slang for the name someone goes by, and on a PC it is what you log in with.

clue.text: Bill fit to be split by men as dear

indicators.note: a thing split by something has it wedged in the middle, so the men go between bill and fit

blocks.note: a bill is a poster, an advert
OR = other ranks, the ordinary soldiers
fit to do something = able to

explanation.surface: An invoice is to be shared among the men, which comes out expensive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dear' looks like the price after all that talk of bills, but it means lovable.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the affectionate sense: a dear child is a lovable one.

clue.text: Fancy boat docks by popular area east of ruin

indicators.note: by means beside, so the two pieces sit side by side
in an across answer east is to the right, so these letters come after the ruin

explanation.surface: Smart moorings are placed near a trendy part of town, east of the ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' belongs to the definition, not the wordplay: it marks this as a smart harbour for yachts rather than a working dock.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a harbour of moorings for pleasure yachts, smarter than a working dock.

clue.text: Do we all cry after beating official warning?

indicators.note: letters that have taken a beating are knocked out of shape

explanation.surface: A question about whether everyone weeps after being thrashed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks a question about tears, but every letter of its first four words is to be shuffled; 'official' is a football referee.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: in football the referee shows this card as a formal caution.

clue.text: Wind model let loose, having a vulgar character

indicators.note: letters let loose are freed from their order and scatter

explanation.surface: A fashion model breaks wind in public, showing her coarse side.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is itself vulgar, which is fair play for a definition about coarseness.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe a coarse, base outlook.

clue.text: Work do

blocks.note: the verb: to function or operate
the verb: to perform a deed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Work do' reads as an office party, but both words are verbs meaning to perform.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are plain synonyms: a drug can work or act, and to do is to act.

clue.text: Brains can get you a chunk of bread

blocks.note: British rhyming slang, where a baked item rhymes with head, and your head holds your brains
a whole baked mass of bread

explanation.surface: Being clever will earn you something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: In British rhyming slang 'use your loaf' means use your head, so the first sense is brains.
explanation.definitionFit: The first sense is rhyming slang for the head and so for intelligence; the second is the ordinary baked item.

clue.text: Female swine hoovering up knight’s cocaine

indicators.note: a vacuum cleaner sucks things inside it, so the pig takes the letter in

blocks.note: a sow is a female pig

explanation.surface: A pig snorts a nobleman's stash of drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hoovering up' is also slang for snorting drugs, which keeps the surface on theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang: the white powder has long been called this, after its look.

clue.text: Love is ...

blocks.note: the surface wants romance; the setter means the tennis score
the dots invite a sweet ending, like the 'Love is...' cartoon captions, but the answer simply completes the equation

explanation.surface: The start of the 'Love is...' cartoon captions, waiting for a tender ending.
explanation.walkthrough: The sentence waits for something sweet, but the answer completes it with tennis scoring, where love means zero.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword staple: in tennis a score of love is zero, so love is literally this.

clue.text: Mooner star fiddled with is one into heavenly bodies

indicators.note: something fiddled with has been tampered with and put out of order

explanation.surface: A celebrity who bares their bottom has been groped by a fan of beautiful bodies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavenly bodies' reads as gorgeous figures, fitting a mooner, but means stars and planets.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: 'into' means keen on, and this scientist studies stars and planets.

clue.text: One covered in whipped cream gets adult in a state

indicators.note: a thing covered in cream is wrapped by it, so the one sits inside
whipped cream has been beaten, so its letters are knocked about

blocks.note: A = adult, the old film certificate

explanation.surface: Someone smothered in whipped cream gets a grown-up into a right state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a state' looks like 'flustered'; only 'a state' is the definition, with 'in' joining it on.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: state here means a nation, and this is one.

clue.text: Power cut around middle of April creates indignation

indicators.note: the power cut goes around, enclosing the letter
the middle of a word is its centre, so take its central letter

explanation.surface: A spring blackout makes people furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like the container instruction, but 'power cut' is a single idea, and 'around' does the enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean angry resentment at something unjust.

clue.text: Online winner is one likely take tenants out

explanation.surface: An internet contest winner is a landlord who throws people out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take out' reads like a date or a hit, but here it means removing tenants from a home.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: this is the person who legally turns tenants out of a property.

clue.text: Clobber a bore for crying out loud!

indicators.note: besides being an exasperated exclamation, it tells you to say the words out loud

blocks.note: to tire someone is to bore them

explanation.surface: Someone exasperated wants to hit a tedious person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clobber' looks like a verb meaning hit but is British slang for clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Regional slang: in Britain clobber means clothes and gear, a casual synonym for formal dress words.

clue.text: GM opening wine and cigar regularly gets complaint

indicators.note: GM opens up after the wine, like a door to the rest
something done regularly happens at even intervals, so take letters at even spacing

blocks.note: Asti is an Italian sparkling wine
second and fourth letters of cIgAr

explanation.surface: A general manager who opens wine and smokes cigars has a grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: The complaint is a medical one, a fault in the eye, not a grumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword staple: complaint also means an ailment, and this is an eye condition, another name for astigmatism.

clue.text: Old artist upset about Girl Guides’ violent behaviour

indicators.note: in a down answer, upset means turned upside down, so read the letters backwards
about means around, so the turned letters go around the guides

explanation.surface: An elderly painter is angry at the girl scouts' rowdy conduct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old artist' looks like one painter, but it is two abbreviations joined and then turned over. Aggro is British slang for trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang: short for aggravation, it means aggressive or violent conduct.

clue.text: Ace loads firearm, primarily overseeing animal release

indicators.note: a gun is loaded by putting something inside it, so the ace goes in
primarily means in the first place, so take the first letter

blocks.note: A = ace in cards, put inside

explanation.surface: A crack shot readies a rifle while supervising the release of a captive animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Animal release' looks like freeing a creature, but it is what birds and bats release: droppings.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: droppings of seabirds and bats are something those animals release.

clue.text: Playing the viola is wasting time aimlessly

blocks.note: a viola is a larger cousin of the violin, and playing any such instrument has a folksy verb

explanation.surface: A jibe that viola practice is a waste of time.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses of fiddle, to play a stringed instrument and to fidget idly, are joined by 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses come from fiddle: to play a violin-family instrument, and to fritter time away.

clue.text: Some Javan titillating Italian's forward

indicators.note: some means a portion, so the answer is a portion of the next words

explanation.surface: A saucy Javanese person teases a pushy Italian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forward' looks like the adjective 'brazen', which fits the titillating surface, but it is the Italian word for 'forward!'
explanation.definitionFit: A foreign word: the Italian for 'forward!' or 'come in!'.

clue.text: My boss steals flipping silver? Blimey!

indicators.note: a thief takes the loot into his keeping, so the boss holds the silver inside
flipping a thing turns it over, so read the silver backwards

blocks.note: the setter's boss is the editor, ED
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: Someone is shocked to find the boss has pinched the silverware.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swear word, which suits the exclamation, but here it turns the silver round.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are dated exclamations of surprise, blimey being British.

clue.text: Where one might see a diver in the open?

blocks.clueFragment: Where one might see a diver
blocks.note: read literally: a high diver is seen in the air over the springboard
the surface suggests an open-air pool; the setter means honest and unconcealed

explanation.surface: Asks where a diver might be spotted outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the open' sounds like a place, an open-air pool, but it means honest and not concealed.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: from card-playing, where hands kept over the table could not cheat, so dealings done this way are open and honest.
